content: The cheroot, also known as the stogie, is a type of cigar that is cylindrical in shape and has both ends clipped during the manufacturing process. Unlike tapered cigars, cheroots are easier and less expensive to roll mechanically, which contributes to their affordability and popularity. Typically, a cheroot measures about 5 inches in length and has a ring gauge of 34 to 37. (The ring gauge is a measure of the cigar's diameter, expressed in 64ths of an inch. For reference, a stogie is slightly over half an inch in diameter.) The term stogie is often misused to describe any cigar with an unpleasant odor. Many stogies are made from flavored tobaccos, and because a stogie can last up to half an hour—compared to the 2–8 minutes of a typical cigarette—it can produce a significant and lingering smell. The word stogie is derived from Conestoga, as these cigars were favored by teamsters who drove Conestoga wagons in the cigar-producing Conestoga Valley region near Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The word cheroot originates from the French term cheroute, which itself is derived from the Tamil words curuttu, churuttu, or shuruttu, meaning roll of tobacco. This term likely entered the French language during the early 16th century, when the French were establishing their presence in South India. From French, the word was subsequently adopted into English. Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, was frequently photographed smoking a stogie. Despite his wife’s disapproval of his smoking habit, Twain often joked about his preference for inexpensive cigars. During one lecture, he humorously claimed that he paid $5 per barrel for his cigars because of his incurable extravagance. In a letter from 1905, later quoted in the March 26, 1911 edition of the New York Times, Twain wrote, I know a good cigar better than you do, for I have had sixty years' experience. No, that is not what I mean; I mean I know a bad cigar better than anybody else. I judge by the price only; if it costs above 5 cents, I know it to be either foreign or half foreign and unsmokable. He also mentioned that he had received many expensive cigars as gifts but never smoked them, instead offering them to visitors. Modern enthusiasts of stogies include figures such as Rush Limbaugh and filmmaker Francis Ford Coppola, who sells his own private-label stogies at his winery. Singer Roger Miller, known for his love of smoking, referenced stogies in his song King of the Road with the line, I smoke old stogies I have found / Short, but not too big around. Cheroots have a historical connection to Asia, particularly in Burma and India, where they were traditional and became popular among the British during the era of the British Empire. In literature, cheroots are often associated with Burma. Additionally, cheroot smoking was believed to offer some resistance to tropical diseases in India. Verrier Elwin, in his 1957 foreword to Leaves from the Jungle: Life in a Gond Village, noted that he frequently fell ill during his non-smoking years but experienced significant health improvements, including the absence of malaria, after taking up cheroot smoking. It is hypothesized that the aroma of the cheroot, by masking the scent of sweat that attracts mosquitoes, may have reduced the smoker's likelihood of being bitten and contracting mosquito-borne diseases such as malaria.
